materials.title: Section II · Part A · Text 1材料
materials.text:
The town of Bellford had a bus service that looked satisfactory on a map. Nearly every neighbourhood was within walking distance of a stop, and the number of buses had remained stable for several years. Yet a residents' survey found that many people considered the service unreliable. Transport planners first assumed that passengers wanted more frequent buses throughout the day. Interviews revealed a more specific problem. Workers on early hospital shifts could reach the main road easily, but the first bus arrived after their shift began. For them, a nearby stop did not amount to usable transport.

Instead of immediately redesigning the whole network, the council ran an eight-week trial. One departure was moved earlier, and a connecting service waited five additional minutes at the station. The changes used the existing vehicles and did not increase the total number of daily departures. Drivers were consulted about the revised breaks, while hospital staff helped choose the arrival time. Posters described the experiment and invited residents to record missed connections. The council wanted to learn not only whether more people boarded a bus, but whether the service allowed them to complete a journey they previously could not make.

Passenger numbers increased during the trial, but the planners resisted claiming that the new timetable explained every extra journey. The hospital had also started a recruitment campaign, and two weeks of heavy rain may have discouraged cycling. They compared early-shift journeys with journeys at other times and asked new passengers how they had travelled before. The evidence suggested a useful improvement, though not a precise estimate of its size. This distinction helped the council discuss the result without promising that the same change would produce identical gains on every route in the town.

The trial was retained, with another review scheduled after six months. Its most valuable lesson was about the definition of access. Distance from a stop mattered, but so did timing, connections, and the purpose of the journey. A simple map could display the first factor and hide the others. By listening to the people who had been counted as well served, the planners discovered a modest change with a practical benefit. They also gained a reason to examine other performance measures before using them as evidence that residents' transport needs had already been met.

materials.title: Section II · Part A · Text 2材料
materials.text:
At a small engineering firm, new apprentices once learned mainly by watching experienced workers and repeating their movements. The method worked well when jobs followed familiar patterns. It was less successful when a machine produced an unusual noise or a component failed a quality check. Some apprentices could perform a standard sequence quickly but could not explain why a particular step was necessary. Their supervisor concluded that speed was an incomplete sign of progress. A learner needed opportunities to describe decisions, diagnose faults, and recognize situations in which the usual procedure should be stopped rather than repeated.

The firm introduced short teaching sessions built around actual workshop problems. An instructor first demonstrated a task while explaining the evidence behind each decision. Apprentices then worked in pairs, with one completing the task and the other asking questions. Their roles changed halfway through the session. The questions were not intended to catch someone making a mistake. They made reasoning audible so that a partner or instructor could identify a misunderstanding before it became a habit. Each session ended with a brief record of what evidence would justify continuing, changing, or stopping the work.

Assessment also changed. A fast performance still counted, but it was considered alongside checks of safety, product quality, and explanation. In one assessment, an instructor deliberately supplied a component with a visible defect. Following the ordinary production steps without noticing it led to a lower score, even if the apprentice finished early. The exercise showed whether the learner could adapt knowledge to the situation. It also sent a clear signal about the firm's priorities: meeting a target did not justify ignoring evidence that the product or the process had become unsafe.

The new approach required time away from immediate production, and some experienced staff initially doubted its value. Their concerns were addressed by keeping sessions short and using faults that had already caused delays. After several months, instructors reported fewer repeated errors, while apprentices asked more precise questions. The firm did not treat these observations as proof that every training method should be replaced. Instead, it planned to track later performance and refine the sessions. The aim was practical competence that could survive a change in circumstances, rather than a performance that looked impressive only when nothing unexpected happened.

materials.title: Section II · Part A · Text 3材料
materials.text:
When volunteers opened a community garden beside an apartment block, they planned equal plots for individual households. The arrangement seemed fair because everyone would receive the same area. During the first summer, however, several plots were barely used. Some residents worked unpredictable hours; others lacked tools or experience. A few enthusiastic gardeners cultivated more produce than their families could eat, while neighbours who wanted vegetables felt unable to take responsibility for a whole plot. The organisers realized that equal space did not necessarily create an equal opportunity to benefit from the garden.

Before changing the rules, they held meetings at different times and distributed a short paper questionnaire. The responses suggested several kinds of participation. Some people wanted independent plots, but others preferred a shared area where they could help occasionally. A retired resident offered to teach beginners, and a nearby café agreed to donate suitable food scraps for compost. The organisers did not assume that every suggestion could be adopted. They listed the labour, costs, and safety arrangements required, then asked volunteers to choose a plan that could be maintained with the people actually available.

The following spring, part of the site became a shared vegetable bed. Visitors could join a weekly session without owning equipment, while experienced gardeners continued to manage individual plots. A notice explained when produce from the shared bed would be distributed and how decisions were made. The system still produced disagreements. Some volunteers contributed more hours than others, and there were questions about which crops should receive scarce water. Having clear rules did not remove these conflicts, but it gave participants a way to discuss them before frustration turned into withdrawal.

At the end of the year, the organisers evaluated the garden through participation, harvest records, and residents' accounts of what they had learned. The number of occupied plots was still useful, but it no longer served as the only measure of success. The project had become more varied without abandoning its original purpose. Its experience suggested that fairness sometimes requires offering different routes into a shared activity. Equal treatment remains an important principle, but applying it well involves asking what people can realistically do, rather than assuming that identical arrangements will have identical effects for everyone.

materials.title: Section II · Part A · Text 4材料
materials.text:
An energy adviser visiting households in a coastal town noticed a repeated misunderstanding. Residents often compared the monthly payment printed on two offers and chose the smaller figure. They reasonably expected a lower payment to mean a lower annual cost. In fact, some offers used a low initial estimate that would be adjusted after the supplier received meter readings. The advertised payment was therefore not always a useful basis for comparing the price of the energy itself. A household could switch expecting savings and later discover that it owed a substantial additional amount.

Working with a local advice centre, the adviser designed a comparison sheet using a household's recent annual consumption. It separated the charge for each unit of energy from the fixed daily charge and showed an estimated yearly total. The sheet also explained that future consumption and prices could change. Instead of presenting the estimate as a promise, advisers used it to make offers comparable under the same assumptions. Residents could then ask whether a different payment schedule or contract condition mattered enough to outweigh a small difference in estimated yearly cost.

The centre tested the sheet in appointments rather than sending it to everyone immediately. Several visitors found the first version difficult because it contained too many figures in equally prominent type. Advisers shortened the sheet, placed the annual comparison near the top, and kept the assumptions visible beside it. They retained the unit prices for people who wanted more detail. This was not simply an attempt to remove information. It was an effort to arrange information so that an important comparison could be made without requiring every visitor to become an expert in energy billing.

Follow-up calls suggested that more residents could explain the difference between a payment estimate and a price. Whether they would save money over a full year remained to be seen, because the final outcome also depended on weather, usage, and contract changes. The centre planned to revisit a sample of households after winter. Its immediate achievement was narrower but useful: people had a clearer basis for choosing and questioning an offer. The experience showed that clear communication is not achieved by making a document short alone. It depends on selecting the right comparison, displaying its assumptions, and checking how readers actually use it.

materials.title: Section II · Part B材料
materials.text:
A neighbourhood repair group wanted to offer a weekly workshop as soon as it found a room. Nadia Ruiz, who helps community groups plan services, asked the organisers to list the people who could reliably attend rather than everyone who had signed up. That left only two dates in the first month. Ruiz thought the limited schedule was useful: it gave visitors a dependable service and let volunteers find out how long each job really took before adding dates.

Getting a service started does not mean that the first visit is easy. Martin Cole described entering a community workshop where he could see the equipment but did not know whether to touch it or who could help. He now asks groups to tell first-time visitors what to bring and to make one person visibly responsible for welcoming them. Once visitors have started a task, they can learn the remaining rules as needed.

Priya Shah agrees that a named contact can help, but she uses lists for a different purpose. At one workshop the same volunteer held the key, contacted visitors, checked the equipment and stayed to lock up. The work was invisible to other members until that person took a holiday. Shah recommends making routine duties visible and reviewing who can take each one; the intention is to enable a handover, not to keep jobs assigned to the same people indefinitely.

What if people stop coming after the first month? Attendance records establish that someone left, says Evan Brooks, but they cannot separate a bus timetable change from dissatisfaction with the workshop. He recommends asking former participants quietly about what made it difficult to return. A difficulty mentioned repeatedly may merit a practical change. Other departures may have nothing to do with the service, so a lower attendance figure is not, on its own, a verdict on quality.

Grace Liu works with groups after they have been running for a term. Some organisers, she says, write an account of decisions before speaking to the volunteers who carry them out. Liu prefers a review in which those volunteers compare the plan with what happens in practice. A meeting is worthwhile if it produces one manageable change and identifies someone to check its effect. An expanding list of general promises is rarely as helpful.

materials.title: Section III · Translation材料
materials.text: A small museum invited local residents to help describe a collection of old photographs. The staff knew when many pictures had been taken, but they could not identify every person or explain every event. Residents brought memories of shops, festivals, and workplaces that no longer existed. Their accounts sometimes disagreed, so the museum recorded who had supplied each description rather than choosing the most confident voice automatically. It also kept the original photographs available for further examination. The project did more than add information to a catalogue. It showed visitors that historical knowledge grows through questions, evidence, and discussion. People who had rarely entered the museum began to see a reason to return. The staff learned that inviting participation did not mean giving up careful research. It meant making the research process more open and allowing new evidence to change an earlier understanding of the past.

source.title: Section II · Part A · Text 1材料
source.exact:
The town of Bellford had a bus service that looked satisfactory on a map. Nearly every neighbourhood was within walking distance of a stop, and the number of buses had remained stable for several years. Yet a residents' survey found that many people considered the service unreliable. Transport planners first assumed that passengers wanted more frequent buses throughout the day. Interviews revealed a more specific problem. Workers on early hospital shifts could reach the main road easily, but the first bus arrived after their shift began. For them, a nearby stop did not amount to usable transport.

Instead of immediately redesigning the whole network, the council ran an eight-week trial. One departure was moved earlier, and a connecting service waited five additional minutes at the station. The changes used the existing vehicles and did not increase the total number of daily departures. Drivers were consulted about the revised breaks, while hospital staff helped choose the arrival time. Posters described the experiment and invited residents to record missed connections. The council wanted to learn not only whether more people boarded a bus, but whether the service allowed them to complete a journey they previously could not make.

Passenger numbers increased during the trial, but the planners resisted claiming that the new timetable explained every extra journey. The hospital had also started a recruitment campaign, and two weeks of heavy rain may have discouraged cycling. They compared early-shift journeys with journeys at other times and asked new passengers how they had travelled before. The evidence suggested a useful improvement, though not a precise estimate of its size. This distinction helped the council discuss the result without promising that the same change would produce identical gains on every route in the town.

The trial was retained, with another review scheduled after six months. Its most valuable lesson was about the definition of access. Distance from a stop mattered, but so did timing, connections, and the purpose of the journey. A simple map could display the first factor and hide the others. By listening to the people who had been counted as well served, the planners discovered a modest change with a practical benefit. They also gained a reason to examine other performance measures before using them as evidence that residents' transport needs had already been met.

source.exact:
At a small engineering firm, new apprentices once learned mainly by watching experienced workers and repeating their movements. The method worked well when jobs followed familiar patterns. It was less successful when a machine produced an unusual noise or a component failed a quality check. Some apprentices could perform a standard sequence quickly but could not explain why a particular step was necessary. Their supervisor concluded that speed was an incomplete sign of progress. A learner needed opportunities to describe decisions, diagnose faults, and recognize situations in which the usual procedure should be stopped rather than repeated.

The firm introduced short teaching sessions built around actual workshop problems. An instructor first demonstrated a task while explaining the evidence behind each decision. Apprentices then worked in pairs, with one completing the task and the other asking questions. Their roles changed halfway through the session. The questions were not intended to catch someone making a mistake. They made reasoning audible so that a partner or instructor could identify a misunderstanding before it became a habit. Each session ended with a brief record of what evidence would justify continuing, changing, or stopping the work.

Assessment also changed. A fast performance still counted, but it was considered alongside checks of safety, product quality, and explanation. source.title: Section II · Part A · Text 3材料
source.exact:
When volunteers opened a community garden beside an apartment block, they planned equal plots for individual households. The arrangement seemed fair because everyone would receive the same area. During the first summer, however, several plots were barely used. Some residents worked unpredictable hours; others lacked tools or experience. A few enthusiastic gardeners cultivated more produce than their families could eat, while neighbours who wanted vegetables felt unable to take responsibility for a whole plot. The organisers realized that equal space did not necessarily create an equal opportunity to benefit from the garden.

Before changing the rules, they held meetings at different times and distributed a short paper questionnaire. The responses suggested several kinds of participation. Some people wanted independent plots, but others preferred a shared area where they could help occasionally. A retired resident offered to teach beginners, and a nearby café agreed to donate suitable food scraps for compost. The organisers did not assume that every suggestion could be adopted. They listed the labour, costs, and safety arrangements required, then asked volunteers to choose a plan that could be maintained with the people actually available.

The following spring, part of the site became a shared vegetable bed. Visitors could join a weekly session without owning equipment, while experienced gardeners continued to manage individual plots. A notice explained when produce from the shared bed would be distributed and how decisions were made. The system still produced disagreements. Some volunteers contributed more hours than others, and there were questions about which crops should receive scarce water. Having clear rules did not remove these conflicts, but it gave participants a way to discuss them before frustration turned into withdrawal.

At the end of the year, the organisers evaluated the garden through participation, harvest records, and residents' accounts of what they had learned. The number of occupied plots was still useful, but it no longer served as the only measure of success. The project had become more varied without abandoning its original purpose. Its experience suggested that fairness sometimes requires offering different routes into a shared activity. Equal treatment remains an important principle, but applying it well involves asking what people can realistically do, rather than assuming that identical arrangements will have identical effects for everyone.

stimulus.text:
A neighbourhood repair group wanted to offer a weekly workshop as soon as it found a room. Nadia Ruiz, who helps community groups plan services, asked the organisers to list the people who could reliably attend rather than everyone who had signed up. That left only two dates in the first month. Ruiz thought the limited schedule was useful: it gave visitors a dependable service and let volunteers find out how long each job really took before adding dates.

Getting a service started does not mean that the first visit is easy. Martin Cole described entering a community workshop where he could see the equipment but did not know whether to touch it or who could help. He now asks groups to tell first-time visitors what to bring and to make one person visibly responsible for welcoming them. Once visitors have started a task, they can learn the remaining rules as needed.

Priya Shah agrees that a named contact can help, but she uses lists for a different purpose. At one workshop the same volunteer held the key, contacted visitors, checked the equipment and stayed to lock up. The work was invisible to other members until that person took a holiday. Shah recommends making routine duties visible and reviewing who can take each one; the intention is to enable a handover, not to keep jobs assigned to the same people indefinitely.

What if people stop coming after the first month? Attendance records establish that someone left, says Evan Brooks, but they cannot separate a bus timetable change from dissatisfaction with the workshop. He recommends asking former participants quietly about what made it difficult to return. A difficulty mentioned repeatedly may merit a practical change. Other departures may have nothing to do with the service, so a lower attendance figure is not, on its own, a verdict on quality.

Grace Liu works with groups after they have been running for a term. Some organisers, she says, write an account of decisions before speaking to the volunteers who carry them out. Liu prefers a review in which those volunteers compare the plan with what happens in practice. A meeting is worthwhile if it produces one manageable change and identifies someone to check its effect. An expanding list of general promises is rarely as helpful.

source.title: Section III · Translation材料
source.exact: A small museum invited local residents to help describe a collection of old photographs. The staff knew when many pictures had been taken, but they could not identify every person or explain every event. Residents brought memories of shops, festivals, and workplaces that no longer existed. Their accounts sometimes disagreed, so the museum recorded who had supplied each description rather than choosing the most confident voice automatically. It also kept the original photographs available for further examination. The project did more than add information to a catalogue. It showed visitors that historical knowledge grows through questions, evidence, and discussion. People who had rarely entered the museum began to see a reason to return. The staff learned that inviting participation did not mean giving up careful research. It meant making the research process more open and allowing new evidence to change an earlier understanding of the past.

questions.prompt: Your university library plans a workshop on evaluating online information. Write an email to a visiting student to invite them. Explain why the workshop is useful, give the time and place (Saturday, 10 a.m., Room 204), and tell them how to register. Sign your name as Li Ming.
questions.solution:
Dear Alex,
I am writing to invite you to a workshop on evaluating online information at our university library. It will be held at 10 a.m. this Saturday in Room 204.
The session will show us how to trace a claim to its original source and compare evidence from different websites. These skills should be useful for both coursework and everyday reading. We will also practise checking a short article together.
If you would like to attend, please reply to this email by Friday afternoon, and I will send your name to the organiser. I hope you can join us.
Best wishes,
Li Ming

questions.prompt: The table shows how students in one university reported using their library in a single month. Borrowing printed books: 2019, 62%; 2025, 48%. Using digital resources: 2019, 45%; 2025, 76%. Using study spaces: 2019, 51%; 2025, 68%. Students could select more than one activity. Write an essay describing the main changes and giving your comments. Do not treat these figures as national statistics.
questions.solution:
The table describes changes in library use at one university between 2019 and 2025. The proportion reporting digital-resource use rose from 45% to 76%, while study-space use increased from 51% to 68%. Printed-book borrowing fell from 62% to 48%, although it remained a substantial activity. Since students could choose several activities, the percentages should not be added together.
These figures suggest that the library's role may be broadening rather than simply declining. Students appear to value both online access and a physical place to work. However, the table alone cannot explain the changes or establish that other universities followed the same pattern.
The university could use the findings to review its balance of collections, digital services, and study areas. Further consultation would help identify what users need. Investment should respond to the range of activities shown, while preserving useful services that a single measure might overlook. This balanced approach would connect resources to documented local needs.
